{{Technical|date=April 2026}}

{{Short description|Self-exciting counting process}}
In probability theory and statistics, a '''Hawkes process''' is an age-dependent [[branching process]] driven by immigration from an inhomogeneous [[Poisson process]].  The process, named after Alan G. Hawkes, is also called a self-exciting [[point process]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Laub |first1=Patrick J. |last2=Lee |first2=Young |last3=Taimre |first3=Thomas |date=2021 |title=The Elements of Hawkes Processes |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-84639-8 |language=en-gb |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-84639-8|isbn=978-3-030-84638-1 |s2cid=245682002 }}</ref>, i.e., the occurrence of an event increases the likelihood of another event occurring. It has arrivals at times <math display=inline> 0 < t_1 < t_2 < t_3 < \cdots </math> where the infinitesimal probability of an arrival during the time interval <math display=inline> [t,t+dt) </math> is

: <math> \lambda_t \, dt = \left( \mu(t) + \sum_{t_k\,:\, t_k\,<\,t} \phi(t-t_k) \right) \, dt. </math>

The function <math display=inline>\mu</math> is the intensity of an underlying [[Poisson process]]. The first arrival occurs at time <math display=inline> t_1</math> and immediately after that, the intensity becomes <math display=inline> \mu(t) + \phi(t-t_1) </math>, and at the time <math display=inline> t_2</math> of the second arrival the intensity jumps to <math display=inline> \mu(t) + \phi(t-t_1) + \phi(t-t_2) </math> and so on.<ref name="Hawkes1971">{{Cite journal |last=Hawkes |first=Alan G. |date=1971 |title=Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/58.1.83 |journal=Biometrika |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.1093/biomet/58.1.83 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

During the time interval <math display=inline> (t_k, t_{k+1}) </math>, the process is the sum of <math display=inline> k+1</math> independent processes with intensities <math display=inline> \mu(t), \phi(t-t_1), \ldots, \phi(t-t_k). </math> The arrivals in the process whose intensity is <math display=inline> \phi(t-t_k) </math> are the "daughters" of the arrival at time <math display=inline> t_k.</math> The integral <math> \int_0^\infty \phi(t)\,dt</math> is the average number of daughters of each arrival and is called the ''branching ratio''. Thus viewing some arrivals as descendants of earlier arrivals, we have a [[Galton–Watson process|Galton–Watson branching process]]. The number of such descendants is finite with probability 1 if branching ratio is 1 or less. If the branching ratio is more than 1, then each arrival has positive probability of having infinitely many descendants.

== Multivariate extension ==

In its seminal paper<ref name="Hawkes1971" />, Hawkes also considered mutually exciting processes which are now called multivariate Hawkes processes. The <math display=inline>  n </math> point processes have arrival times denoted by <math display=inline> 0 < t^i_1 < t^i_2 < t^i_3 < \cdots </math> for each type <math display=inline> i=1,\dots, n </math>. The probability of shared points is null, i.e. <math display=inline> \mathbb{P}(\exists (i,k) \neq (j,\ell): t^i_k = t^j_\ell ) =0 </math>, and for each <math display=inline> i</math>, the infinitesimal probability of an arrival of type <math display=inline> i</math> during the time interval <math display=inline> [t,t+dt) </math> is

: <math> \lambda^i_t \, dt = \left( \mu_i(t) + \sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{t^j_k\,:\, t^j_k\,<\,t} \phi_{ij}(t-t^j_k) \right) \, dt. </math>

The interaction is now described by a matrix of functions <math display=inline> \mathbf{\Phi} = (\phi_{ij})_{1\leq i,j \leq n}</math> and the matrix integral <math> \int_0^\infty \mathbf{\Phi}(t)\,dt</math> plays the role of branching ratio.

== Density-dependent extension ==

Brémaud and Massoulié extended Hawkes processes to allow for a density-dependent birth-rate. They considered an infinitesimal probability of arrival of the following form: 

:<math> \lambda_t \, dt = f\left( \mu(t) + \sum_{t_k\,:\, t_k\,<\,t} \phi(t-t_k) \right) \, dt, </math>

for some non-negative function <math>f</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brémaud |first1=Pierre |last2=Massoulié |first2=Laurent |title=Stability of nonlinear Hawkes processes |journal=The Annals of Probability |date=1 July 1996 |volume=24 |issue=3 |doi=10.1214/aop/1065725193}}</ref> The original density-independent Hawkes process thus corresponds to <math>f(x)=x</math>. Of course, both density-dependent and multivariate extensions are possible at the same time.  While this density-dependent extension of the Hawkes process is still a point process, it is no longer a branching process because point offspring distributions are no longer independent.

This density-dependent extension allows for negative propensities <math>\phi</math>. Hence it can model self-inhibition or mutual inhibition (in a multivariate context) which can be important in neuroscience <ref>{{cite book |last1=Reynaud-Bouret |first1=Patricia |last2=Rivoirard |first2=Vincent |last3=Tuleau-Malot |first3=Christine |chapter=Inference of functional connectivity in Neurosciences via Hawkes processes |title=2013 IEEE Global Conference on Signal and Information Processing |date=December 2013 |pages=317–320 |doi=10.1109/GlobalSIP.2013.6736879 |bibcode=2013glob.conf...93R |isbn=978-1-4799-0248-4 }}</ref>.

== Applications ==
Hawkes processes are used for statistical modeling of events in [[mathematical finance]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hawkes |first=Alan G. |date=2018 |title=Hawkes processes and their applications to finance: a review |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/14697688.2017.1403131 |journal=Quantitative Finance |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=193–198 |doi=10.1080/14697688.2017.1403131 |bibcode=2018QuFin..18..193H |s2cid=158619662 |issn=1469-7688|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[epidemiology]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rizoiu |first1=Marian-Andrei |last2=Mishra |first2=Swapnil |last3=Kong |first3=Quyu |last4=Carman |first4=Mark |last5=Xie |first5=Lexing |date=2018 |chapter=SIR-Hawkes: Linking Epidemic Models and Hawkes Processes to Model Diffusions in Finite Populations |arxiv=1711.01679 |title=Proceedings of the 2018 World Wide Web Conference on World Wide Web - WWW '18 |pages=419–428 |doi=10.1145/3178876.3186108|s2cid=195346881 }}</ref> earthquake [[seismology]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kwon |first1= Junhyeon |last2= Zheng |first2= Yingcai |last3=Jun|first3=Mikyoung|date=2023 |title=Flexible spatio-temporal Hawkes process models for earthquake occurrences |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spasta.2023.100728|journal=Spatial Statistics |volume=54 |article-number= 100728 |doi=10.1016/j.spasta.2023.100728|arxiv=2210.08053 |bibcode= 2023SpaSt..5400728K |s2cid= 252917746 }}</ref> and other fields in which a random event exhibits self-exciting behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tench |first1=Stephen |last2=Fry |first2=Hannah |last3=Gill |first3=Paul |date=2016 |title=Spatio-temporal patterns of IED usage by the Provisional Irish Republican Army |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-journal-of-applied-mathematics/article/abs/spatiotemporal-patterns-of-ied-usage-by-the-provisional-irish-republican-army/3BC0D8552313F1BC893D5F6519079BB8 |journal=European Journal of Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=377–402 |doi=10.1017/S0956792515000686 |s2cid=53692006 |issn=0956-7925|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Laub |first1=Patrick J. |last2=Taimre |first2=Thomas |last3=Pollett |first3=Philip K. |date=2015 |title=Hawkes Processes |class=math.PR |eprint=1507.02822 }}</ref>
